note: Which regular-expression constructs Find accepts, pinned once for both views (#5 F-6).
for a refused row and a Regex for an accepted one) and by editor-src/test/find.test.mjs
(an accepted row must compile as `new RegExp(pattern, 'gmu')` and index without error;
a refused row is checked against its own 'refusedBy', below).
The rule: a pattern must mean the same thing in both views or be refused outright, with
the same 'Invalid pattern.' message Find already shows. A refused row is NOT necessarily
one JavaScript rejects — EITHER engine may be the one that refuses it, and some are
refused by the host although both engines compile them. Each refused row says which,
and find.test.mjs asserts that much of it as the browser engine can answer for (#5 NF-6):
refusedBy 'javascript' — JavaScript will not compile it; find.test.mjs checks that.
refusedBy 'dotnet'     — .NET will not compile it and JavaScript will; find.test.mjs
checks that it does compile here, which is why the host has
refusedBy 'host'       — both engines compile it today and read it differently (or not
every browser has it): only FindEngine.JsCompatible refuses it,
and only FindEngineTests can prove that.

literals.why: a space: the escape .NET writes for one, '\ ', is not an escape JavaScript has
a hash: same story as the space
a dash stays as it is: '\-' outside a class is an error in JavaScript

accepted.why: a dash at the end of a class is literal in both
named group and the backreference spelling both engines share
a named group written AFTER every unnamed one leaves the numbering alone: \1 is (x) in both
with no unnamed group there is nothing to reorder: \1 is the named group in both
all-named groups are numbered in source order by both engines
a one-letter Unicode category, spelled the same in both
a two-letter Unicode category, spelled the same in both

refused.why: \A is .NET's start-of-string anchor; JavaScript has no such escape
\Z is .NET's end-of-string anchor
\z is .NET's absolute end anchor
\G anchors to where the last match ended; .NET only
atomic group; .NET only
inline options for the rest of the pattern; .NET only, and they would silently change the search
inline options on a group: .NET has always had them and JavaScript only lately, so a browser without them refuses the search the source view runs
inline options turned off on a group: same story as (?i:...)
class subtraction: .NET subtracts, and under the unicode flag JavaScript refuses the pattern outright (it is the NON-unicode mode that reads it as a union)
possessive quantifier; .NET only
possessive quantifier
possessive quantifier
possessive quantifier
comment group; .NET only
.NET's other spelling of a named group

a named group written BEFORE an unnamed one reorders the numbers: .NET numbers the unnamed groups first, so \1 is (y) there and (?<a>x) here — the pattern matches 'xyy' in the source view and 'xyx' in the formatted one, and both engines compile it (#5 NF-1)
balancing group; .NET only
.NET's other spelling of a named backreference
conditional; .NET only
a Unicode BLOCK name; JavaScript spells blocks differently
the long category name is JavaScript's: .NET knows only \p{L} and \p{Lu} and refuses 'Letter' as an unknown property
a brace that starts no quantifier is literal in .NET and an error in JavaScript
a loose closing brace is literal in .NET and an error in JavaScript
a loose closing bracket is literal in .NET and an error in JavaScript
\a is .NET's bell character
\e is .NET's escape character
an escaped dash outside a class is literal in .NET and an error in JavaScript
the code-point escape is JavaScript's: .NET reads \u as exactly four hex digits and refuses the braces
